Let’s dive into Chapter 7: Building Ownership and Accountability — The Investor Discipline.
You know, the heart of the Investor discipline is all about giving others the space, resources, and trust they need to succeed. Multipliers—those leaders who really get the best out of people—understand that folks grow the most when they’re handed real ownership and are trusted to deliver meaningful results.
So, what does it look like to be an Investor, not just a manager? Well, Investors don’t hover or micromanage. Instead, they give clear direction, make sure their team has what they need, and then step back. They’re still there if someone needs support, but the message is clear: You’ve got this. And that confidence? It sparks a strong sense of ownership.
Let’s break down some key practices that set Investors apart.
First, they delegate real responsibility. They’re not just handing out busywork. Instead, they assign important projects and make it clear that the outcome truly matters. The team knows they’re being trusted to deliver.
Second, Investors provide resources and support. Sure, they step back from the daily grind, but they don’t just disappear. Maybe they connect someone with a mentor, secure the budget, or help cut through red tape. Whatever it is, they make sure the team has what they need to succeed.
Third, they set clear expectations. There’s no guessing about what success looks like or how progress will be measured. Everyone’s on the same page, and priorities are crystal clear.
And just as important, Investors hold people accountable. They check in on commitments, offer feedback—both the good and the tough stuff—and celebrate wins. If something falls short, it’s a chance to learn and get better, not just a reason for criticism.
Picture this: a senior leader gives a rising team member the chance to lead a big client presentation. The leader offers some advice on key points, makes sure the data is available, then steps back and lets that team member shine during both prep and delivery. Afterward, they sit down together to talk about what worked, and where to grow next time. That’s the Investor approach in action.
Now, compare that to a Diminisher—a leader who only delegates trivial tasks, micromanages every detail, or fails to give the right support. People end up feeling overwhelmed or just plain underused. And that kind of environment? It stunts both growth and engagement.
The Investor discipline is about building a cycle of trust, ownership, and accountability. When people are trusted with real responsibility and given what they need to succeed, they step up—and the whole team gets stronger.
So, if you want your team to grow and thrive, remember: trust them, support them, and let them own their results. That’s how you create leaders at every level.
